newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil's telecom law completes Congress dash.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil's telecom law completes Congress dash.

text.p: Brazil's plan to privatize its huge telecommunications sector gathered more steam Thursday when a bill allowing the sale of federal holding Telebras completed its sprint through Congress.

Unlike key structural reforms, which have been bogged down in parliament for more than two years, the General Telecommunications Law took just four months from first discussions in the lower house to final approval in the Senate.

Analysts said the speed of the bill showed the government was determined to meet its target of beginning the Telebras sell-off next year, starting with the privatization of Telesp in Sao Paulo state, valued at $25 billion, and long-distance carrier Embratel.
"They're doing everything right and quickly too," said Vera Rosa Rossi, an analyst with ING Barings in Sao Paulo.
Lawmakers said Thursday's approval of the new law removed the last political hurdle in the way of privatization.

"Now we are in a position to enter the third millenium," said Senator Hugo Napoleao, a former communications minister, shortly after the upper house of parliament approved the bill. The legislation now requires the signature of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso before coming into effect.

Approval of the bill came a day after a consortium led by BellSouth and Brazilian bank Banco Safra bid $2.45 billion for a cellular telephone contract in Sao Paulo city, more than four times the government's asking price.
Another, smaller concession went to a group led by Italy's STET which paid 250 million reais for a contract in the northeastern states of Bahia and Sergipe.
"The government is putting its foot on the gas," said a telecommunications analyst who asked not to be named. "The next big important step is the creation of the regulator."

The law approved Thursday gives the government 90 days to set up the National Telecommunications Agency (ANATEL), a new regulator linked to the Communications Ministry, but with administrative independence and its own budget.
ANATEL will have powers to ensure competition in the telecommunications sector. It will also control rates for an initial three-year period.
British consultants Coopers & Lybrand are currently advising the Communications Ministry on how to set up the regulator.

With ANATEL in place, the government will convince would-be private sector operators that they will be free to do business without the kind of political interference that has hampered Telebras since its inception, analysts say.
An official said Thursday the Communications Ministry would begin shortly the process of hiring international consultants to draw up a model for the sale of the Telebras system.

The government is expected to group the holding's 27 sudsidiaries into four regional companies and then privatize them. Telesp, the biggest of the subsidiaries, would probably be sold alone or with its own unit, Companhia Telefonica Borda do Campo, which operates on the outskirts of Sao Paulo city.
Another contract to advise on the asking price for Telesp and Embratel would probably be tendered by the end of 1997, the official said.
